title: Valuation Builder: DCF process
description: One complete valuation-process exercise: build a DCF from forecast to implied share price, with distractors, parallel branches and two accepted terminal value methods.

valuationExercises.title: Build a DCF valuation process
valuationExercises.task: Build the process for valuing a company with an unlevered DCF, from the operating forecast to the implied value per share, using one terminal value method.
instructions: Drag the steps you need from the bank onto the canvas, then draw an arrow from each step to the step that depends on it, so an arrow means 'this must be done before that'.

The bank also holds steps that do not belong in this process. Steps that do not depend on each other should not be chained one after another: show them as parallel branches that join where both are needed.

assumptions.label: Approach
assumptions.value: Unlevered free cash flows discounted at WACC to enterprise value

assumptions.label: Terminal value
assumptions.value: Use either the perpetuity growth or the exit multiple method, not both

steps.label: Forecast revenue and operating profit (EBIT)
steps.explanation: Every cash flow in the DCF is built from an operating forecast, so this is the starting point.

steps.label: Tax-effect EBIT to get NOPAT
steps.explanation: Unlevered cash flow starts from operating profit after tax, before any interest. NOPAT = EBIT x (1 - tax rate).

steps.label: Add back D&A; deduct capex and the increase in net working capital
steps.explanation: Depreciation is non-cash, while capital spending and working capital absorb cash. Both are driven by the operating forecast.

steps.label: Calculate unlevered free cash flow
steps.explanation: NOPAT plus D&A, less capex and the increase in net working capital gives the cash flow available to all capital providers.

steps.label: Calculate WACC
steps.explanation: The discount rate for unlevered cash flows is the weighted average cost of capital. It depends on the capital structure and market inputs, not on the forecast, so it can be built in parallel.

steps.label: Calculate terminal value (perpetuity growth)
steps.explanation: Values the cash flows beyond the forecast by growing the final-year cash flow at a steady rate.

steps.label: Calculate terminal value (exit multiple)
steps.explanation: Values the business at the end of the forecast by applying a market multiple to final-year EBITDA. An alternative to the perpetuity growth method.

steps.label: Discount the projected cash flows at WACC
steps.explanation: Each forecast year's unlevered free cash flow is brought back to today at WACC.

steps.label: Discount the terminal value at WACC
steps.explanation: The terminal value sits at the end of the forecast, so it is discounted back to today at WACC as well.

steps.label: Add the present values to get enterprise value
steps.explanation: Enterprise value is the present value of the forecast cash flows plus the present value of the terminal value.

steps.label: Calculate net debt
steps.explanation: Debt less cash from the balance sheet. It does not depend on the forecast, so it can be done in parallel.

steps.label: Subtract net debt to get equity value
steps.explanation: Enterprise value belongs to all capital providers; subtracting net debt leaves the value attributable to shareholders.

steps.label: Calculate diluted shares outstanding
steps.explanation: Shares plus the dilution from options and convertibles. It is independent of the valuation steps and is needed only at the end.

steps.label: Divide equity value by diluted shares
steps.explanation: Equity value per diluted share is the implied share price, the end point of the process.

steps.label: Calculate levered free cash flow (after interest and debt repayment)
steps.explanation: Does not belong. Levered cash flow is for an equity-value DCF; this process discounts unlevered cash flow at WACC to reach enterprise value.

steps.label: Discount the cash flows at the cost of equity
steps.explanation: Does not belong. Unlevered cash flows are discounted at WACC. The cost of equity only suits cash flows that belong to shareholders alone.

steps.label: Add net debt to enterprise value to get equity value
steps.explanation: Does not belong. The bridge runs the other way: equity value = enterprise value minus net debt.

steps.label: Apply peer trading multiples to current EBITDA
steps.explanation: Does not belong. That is a trading comparables valuation, a different method from a DCF.

steps.label: Start from the book value of equity
steps.explanation: Does not belong. A DCF values the cash flows of the business; book value is an accounting figure from the balance sheet.

steps.label: Deduct interest expense before taxing EBIT
steps.explanation: Does not belong. Unlevered cash flow ignores financing, so interest is not deducted; the tax shield is captured in WACC.
